check.question: Contour lines packed close together mean the ground is…
check.why: Close lines mean the height changes quickly over a short distance, which is a steep slope.

steps: A contour line joins points on the map that are at the same height.
Where contour lines crowd close together the ground is steep; where they spread apart it is gentle.
Open the map and find the lookout trail: it climbs where the lines are spread, not straight up where they crowd.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Reading contour lines
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A trail crew reads the contours to plan a route that avoids the steepest ground.

check.question: Two places look twice as far apart on the map as two others. On the ground that walk is…
check.why: One scale for the whole map means map distance and ground distance grow together.

steps: A map's scale says how much ground one step on the map stands for.
This map is square and every place on it is drawn at the same scale, so equal map distances are equal walks anywhere on it.
Pick two places on the map, guess which walk is longer, then read the distance the HUD shows as you go.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Map scale and distance
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A road crew measures a work zone off the plan sheet with its scale before a cone goes down.

check.question: Water behind a dam stores energy mainly because of its…
check.why: The higher the water sits above the turbine, the more energy it can give up on the way down.

steps: Water held high behind a dam has stored energy because of its height.
As it falls through the penstock that energy becomes motion.
The moving water spins a turbine, and the turbine turns a generator that makes electrical energy.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Falling water as stored energy
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A powerhouse operator watches water's stored energy become electrical energy, the same chain the wind farm follows with air.

options: Water pressure is greatest at the bottom
To save concrete at the top only
check.question: Why is a dam thicker at the bottom?
check.why: The deepest water pushes hardest, so the wall needs the most strength at its base.

steps: Water pushes on everything in it, and the deeper you go the more water sits above you.
That is why a dam wall is built thicker at the bottom than at the top.
Look at the dam's face: it widens toward its base, where the push of the water is greatest.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Pressure grows with depth
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A diver clearing a dam intake and the engineer who designed the wall both plan for pressure that grows with depth.

check.question: Snow on the summit reaches the reservoir mainly by…
check.why: Meltwater flows the way the river below the powerhouse does: down, into the streams and the reservoir.

steps: Water evaporates, condenses into clouds and falls as rain or snow on the mountain.
Snowmelt and rain run downhill into streams and the reservoir.
At the treatment plant the water is filtered and disinfected before it goes to homes: the plant is one stop on the water cycle, not its end.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: From snowpack to tap
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A water treatment operator treats the reservoir water that the mountain's snow and rain supply.

options: It stops flowing in that circuit
check.question: What happens to current when a breaker opens the circuit?
check.why: With the loop broken there is no path for current, which is what the crew then proves with a tester.

steps: Current only flows around a complete loop, a closed circuit.
Opening a switch or a breaker breaks the loop, so current stops.
That is why the switching order opens the circuit first, and then the crew proves it is dead before they touch it.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: A complete circuit
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A substation electrician opens a breaker to break a circuit before anyone works on it.

options: On its label and data sheet
check.question: Where does the crew find the protection a chemical needs?
check.why: The label and data sheet are written for exactly that chemical; a guess is not.

steps: A hazard label names the chemical, shows pictograms and a signal word, and says how to protect yourself.
The label and the safety data sheet, not memory, say what protective equipment the job needs.
Before any delivery, the crew reads the label on the load and matches it to the paperwork.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Reading a hazard label
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A plant operator reads a chemical's label and data sheet before a delivery is unloaded.

check.question: A road rises the same height over a shorter run. Its grade is…
check.why: Grade is rise divided by run, so a shorter run for the same rise gives a bigger ratio.

steps: A road's grade is how much it rises for each unit it runs forward.
The same rise over half the run is twice as steep.
The HUD shows the slope under your feet: compare the climb here with the flatter road beside the yard.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Grade as a ratio
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A driver reads a grade as rise over run, and the pass road's signs state it the same way.

options: Opinions about who is to blame
check.question: A good report sticks to…
check.why: A report is evidence for someone who was not there, so it carries only what was seen.

steps: A clear report says what happened, where, when and who was involved.
It sticks to what the writer saw, and says plainly what they do not know yet.
From the lookout, write a one-line report of something you can see: the place, the time on the HUD clock, and what it is.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Writing a clear trail report
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A ranger writes what they saw, where and when: facts first, no guesses.

check.question: What should you say first when calling for help?
check.why: Help can only come once it knows where to go.

steps: When someone is hurt, make sure you are safe, then call for help.
Say where you are first, a named place like the gondola top station, so help can find you.
Stay on the line and do what the call-taker asks.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Calling for help on the mountain
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A lift attendant gives a clear location first when they call for help.

options: The same meter is used in the same place
Different meters are used to be safe
One is taken outside in the sun
check.question: Two air readings are only comparable when…
check.why: Changing the meter or the spot changes more than one thing, so the difference could be the meter, not the air.

steps: A fair test changes one thing at a time and keeps everything else the same.
The heading crew reads the air at the face before the ventilation runs and again after, with the same meter in the same place.
Only then can they say the fans made the difference, and the plan says what reading lets work go on.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Testing the air is a fair test
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A tunnel crew tests the air with the same meter, at the same spot, before and after the fans run, so the two readings can be compared.

options: Put the events in the order they happened
check.question: To build a timeline from documents you first…
check.why: Order is what a timeline adds; every document is evidence for where an event sits on it.

steps: A timeline puts events in the order they happened, with the evidence for each.
The portal crew's shift log, the concrete delivery tickets and the survey notes are three documents about the same day.
Put them in order and the day tells its own story: what was sprayed, when the survey checked it, and what came next.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: The shift log is a timeline
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A heading boss rebuilds what happened on a shift from the log, the delivery tickets and the survey notes, in time order.

options: A guess from the road edge
check.question: Which is the primary source for where a buried line is?
check.why: First-hand evidence gathered on the day outranks a copy of an older record.

steps: A primary source is first-hand evidence; a secondary source describes or copies it.
At the portal trench the locator's paint on the ground is first-hand: it was found with an instrument today. The old drawing is a copy of what someone once recorded.
When the two disagree, the crew trusts the marks, and exposes the line by hand before the bucket goes near it.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Marks on the ground and lines on the drawing
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: An operator treats the locator's marks on the ground as the primary source and the drawing as secondary, and digs by hand where they disagree.

check.question: On the gondola drive, the haul rope is moved by…
check.why: The rope rides on the bullwheel, so the wheel's turn is the rope's travel.

steps: A wheel and axle is a simple machine: turning one turns the other, and the bigger part moves further for each turn.
In the drive room the motor turns the axle and the big bullwheel carries the haul rope around.
The brake grips the wheel, which is why the brake test is done before any cabin carries a person.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: The bullwheel is a wheel and axle
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A lift mechanic sees the drive as a wheel and axle: the motor turns the axle, the big wheel moves the rope, and the brake holds the wheel.

options: So the drive cannot start until every one of them is done
To make the lockout look tidy
Because one lock is not strong enough
check.question: Why does each mechanic hang their own lock?
check.why: A lock per person means no one can be forgotten inside the machine when it is restarted.

steps: Good teamwork means each person does their part and checks a partner's part without blame.
In the drive room each mechanic hangs their own lock on the isolation point, so nothing can start until every lock is off.
Then they check each other's lock and tag and say what they found, which is feedback the job depends on.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Two people, one lockout
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A lift crew locks out the drive with each person's own lock, and each checks the other's before work starts.

options: Measuring it and comparing with the plan's limit
Looking at the colour of the sky
check.question: The crew decides the wind is too strong for the lift by…
check.why: A limit written in the plan is only useful when the wind is actually measured against it.

steps: Wind, cloud and temperature are what a weather reading is made of, and each can be read from where you stand.
At the top station, feel the wind, watch which way the cloud moves and how fast, and read the temperature the HUD shows.
Lift and rigging plans set a wind limit; the crew does not guess at it, they measure and compare.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Reading the sky before the lift opens
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A lift operator and a rigger both read the wind and the cloud before a cabin or a load leaves the ground, and the plan says when they stop.

options: Hold its shape under a push
check.question: Bracing a frame into triangles makes it…
check.why: A triangle's angles are fixed by its sides, so the frame cannot lean without stretching or breaking a member.

steps: A square frame can lean over and fold; a triangle cannot change shape without a side changing length.
Look up at the tower legs: every panel is braced into triangles, and each brace meets a leg at an angle the drawing sets.
That is why a climber's anchor point is a braced member, and the climb plan names which ones.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Triangles hold a tower up
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A tower climber clips to members braced into triangles, the shape that does not fold under a push.

options: Water held high behind the dam
check.question: The energy in the ridge line's wires began as…
check.why: Follow the chain backwards: wire, generator, turbine, penstock, reservoir.

steps: Energy is not made from nothing; it moves from one form and one place to another.
Water falling through the penstock becomes motion in a turbine, then electrical energy in a generator, then current in the wires you can see overhead.
The substation changes the voltage so the line can carry it a long way with less loss, and the switching crew is the last hand on that chain.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Where the ridge's power goes
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A lineworker follows the energy from the powerhouse to the substation and along the ridge line as one chain of transfers.

options: The listener understood the same message
check.question: A read-back proves that…
check.why: Only hearing the message repeated shows it arrived as it was meant.

steps: Clear speaking is one message at a time, in a steady voice, with the important word first.
On the radio the operator gives the step, the other person repeats it back, and only a matching read-back means it was understood.
Practise here: say the name of this site and the next site on your map as if the listener could not see you.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Say it once, clearly, and hear it back
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A switching operator speaks each order plainly and waits for the read-back before the next step.

options: It can be repeated the same way next time
It covers the whole mountain at once
check.question: A transect count is useful because…
check.why: Repeating the same line the same way is what makes two counts comparable.

steps: A transect is a straight line through a habitat; you walk it and record what you find at set points along it.
Under the ridge line the crew notes which plants are growing back toward the wires and where the ground is bare.
The same count next season shows what changed, and the vegetation plan says what needs clearing.
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.title: Counting life along a line
SM_FIELD_LESSONS.tradeLine: A right-of-way patroller walks the line and records what grows under it, the same transect method a kelp survey uses under water.

steps.text: Check in at the valley base muster board.
Walk up the valley road to the treatment plant.
Run the chlorine room changeout from the plant's job board.
Follow the service road up to the dam.
Lock out the intake before the screen is cleaned.
Sign the trail register at the ranger station.
Hike to the West Ridge Lookout.
Report to the pass road crew yard.
Ride the switchbacks with the crew and set the engine brake at the pull-out.
Take the mountain grade the way the sign says.
Drive or walk up to the tunnel portal.
Clear the crew and shoot the portal face.
Switch the substation with an order and a read-back.
Climb to the ridge line crew's pad.
Lock out the drive and test the brake.
Stand at the summit lookout and pick out every site you worked.

advice.text: The pull-out before a long grade is where the brakes are checked, while it is still easy to stop: the air pressure built and holding, the engine brake switched on so it is ready the moment you lift off the throttle, and the mirrors set to show the trailer tandems, because smoke from a hot brake shows there before you smell it.

SM_RIDES.blurb: Board the crew pickup at the yard. It climbs the switchbacks and stops at the pass saddle's pull-out: set the engine brake there (E) before it starts down to the tunnel portal. Setting it on the grade scores less; not setting it at all costs more than the arrival is worth.
SM_RIDES.name: Ride the Pass With the Crew
